1:1: The word Ramathaim Zophim is the name of a city. This is the same city that the author calls Ramah in the rest of the book. See the discussion in the Introduction to 1 Samuel of why he uses a different name here.
1:3: The author is speaking of Elkanah to mean him and his entire family. The text makes clear in the next two verses that his wives and children accompanied him.
1:4: The author is using the term day to represent a specific time or occasion.
1:5: The author is using one part of two people, their faces, to mean the people themselves.
The author is using the idea of a womb opening to release a child into the world to mean the ability to have children.
1:6: For emphasis, the author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
The author assumes that readers will know that by her adversary, he means Peninnah.
The author is speaking as if Hannah would actually thunder. He means that Peninnah would try to make her so upset that she would speak loudly and emotionally.
1:7: The author assumes that readers will know that by thus he did, he means that Elkanah gave portions to his wives and children as he has described.
1:8: Elkanah is using the question form for emphasis.
Elkanah is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Hannah feeling badly. He does not mean that she is entertaining any wrong thoughts.
1:9: While in this context the term arose could refer to getting up from sitting or reclining at a table for a meal, the author could be using it here to mean that Hannah took action to address her situation by going to the tent of meeting and praying to the Lord.
Elkanah assumes that readers will know that by after eating and after drinking he means after the others had finished eating and drinking. He said in verse 7 that Hannah herself did not eat.
וְעֵלִי הַכֹּהֵן יֹשֵׁב עַל־הַכִּסֵּא עַל־מְזוּזַת הֵיכַל יְהוָה
The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
Sitting by the doorpost was a symbolic action that indicated that Eli, as a priest, would listen to people’s concerns and try to address them.
See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of why the author uses the term temple here.
1:10: The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Hannah was deeply distressed. He does not mean that she was harboring any feelings of bitterness or thoughts of revenge.
1:11: The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
The terms remember and not forget mean similar things. Hannah is using the two terms together for emphasis.

Hannah is speaking as if the Lord actually needs to be reminded of her. In contexts such as this, the term remember describes the Lord thinking about a person or group and considering what action he can take on their behalf. It does not suggest that God ever forgets about people.
Hannah is using the term days to represent a specific time, Samuel’s lifetime.
This is an expression that people of this culture commonly used to describe cutting the hair on a person’s head.
Not cutting one’s hair was a symbolic action that indicated a vow of dedication to the Lord.
1:12: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two verbs together. The verb made much tells in what way Hannah prayed.
See the discussion of the phrase to the face of in the Introduction to 1 Samuel. Here, to the face of represents being in the presence of the Lord.
1:13: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
1:14: Eli is using the question form for emphasis.
1:15: Hannah is speaking as if her soul were a liquid that she could pour out. She means that she has been expressing her deepest feelings to the Lord.
Hannah is using one part of herself, her soul, to mean all of herself in the act of praying.
1:16: Hannah is speaking as if Eli might put her in front of a daughter of wickedness, meaning that he might make her a servant or slave of such a person. This represents Eli thinking that Hannah was such a person.
In certain contexts, the biblical text uses the expression daughter of to indicate that a person shares the qualities of something. That is the case here.
Hannah is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it.
1:17: As the Introduction to 1 Samuel discusses, Eli is using the name Israel to represent his descendants.
Eli is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
1:18: Hannah ate as a symbolic action that showed she was no longer too distressed to eat.
1:19: The author is speaking in a polite way about a private matter.
1:20: לִתְקֻפוֹת הַיָּמִים וַתַּהַר חַנָּה וַתֵּלֶד בֵּן

The author is using a common expression of his culture to describe one period of time ending and another one beginning. This could mean: (1) that the author, as in 1:3, is using the plural form days to mean a year; (2) that the author is referring to Hannah’s pregnancy reaching full term and ending in childbirth. In that case, he would mean that she conceived to begin this period and that she bore a son at the end of it.
1:21: The author is using the term house to represent Elkanah’s family.
The author is making an overstatement for emphasis. He means that most of Elkanah’s family went with him. The next verse explains that Hannah did not go with him on this occasion.
The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
See the discussion of the term vow here in the Introduction to this chapter.
1:22: When Hannah says he will be seen, she is using a common expression of her culture. This is similar to the expression “was found” in 13:22. If something was seen or was found in a place, this means that it was in that place.

Hannah is using the term face to represent the Lord’s presence. While the usual expression is “to the face,” here Hannah says at the face, perhaps to describe Samuel coming into the Lord’s presence and remaining there.
1:23: Elkanah is speaking as if the Lord’s word were an object that the Lord could raise up to a high position. He means that he wants the Lord to fulfill what he has promised.
The author is using the term word to represent what the Lord promised by using words, speaking through Eli.
1:24: בְּפָרִים שְׁלֹשָׁה וְאֵיפָה אַחַת קֶמַח וְנֵבֶל יַיִן
The author assumes that readers will know that Hannah brought these things to be used as sacrifices.
This ephah was equivalent to 22 liters or nearly six gallons.
The author is speaking as if the Lord actually lived in a house. This was a way of describing the tent of meeting, where the Lord was present.
The author is providing background information to help readers understand an important detail in the story. He means that Samuel, the boy, was still very young, only a little boy.
1:25: The author assumes that readers will know that by the bull, he means one of the three bulls that Hannah brought. The family had decided to sacrifice this particular one as a whole burnt offering to consecrate Samuel to the Lord’s service.
1:26: Following the custom of her culture, Hannah is swearing an oath by guaranteeing it by something she holds sacred, the life of the Lord’s high priest.
Hannah is using one part of Eli, his soul, to mean all of him.
1:28: The author is using the term days to represent a period of time, Samuel’s lifetime.
2:1: עָלַץ לִבִּי בַּיהוָה רָמָה קַרְנִי בַּיהוָה

See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of how Hebrew poetry frequently uses pairs of phrases that mean basically the same thing, in which the second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first phrase by repeating the same idea in different words.
Hannah is using one part of her, her heart, representing her thoughts and feelings, to mean all of her in the act of rejoicing.

Hannah is speaking as if she were an animal that had a horn that she could life up high. An animal that lifts its horn is demonstrating strength and assertiveness. Accordingly, in this culture, a horn represented strength and dignity.
Hannah is using the idea of opening her mouth wide to represent speaking boldly.
Hannah assumes that readers will know that by enemies she means people such as Peninnah, who has mocked her for being childless.
2:2: Hannah is speaking as if God were a rock. She means that he provides protection and security, just as people could find safety by climbing up on a high rock or by hiding among rocks.
2:3: אַל־תַּרְבּוּ תְדַבְּרוּ גְּבֹהָה גְבֹהָה יֵצֵא עָתָק מִפִּיכֶם

Hannah is speaking to people who are not present, particularly Peninnah, who had mocked her for being childless. She is doing this to show in a very strong way how she feels about their arrogant behavior.

Hannah is using a common expression of her culture to mean that people should stop speaking arrogantly. She does not mean that arrogant words should go out from the mouth of these people in the sense that they should speak them. She means that those words should not be in their mouths, that is, they should not speak them.
Hannah is speaking as if actions were objects that could be weighed on a scale. She means that the Lord evaluates everything that people do.
2:4: Hannah assumes that readers will know that by the stumbling ones, she means people who are so weak that they can barely walk.
Hannah is speaking as if strength were a piece of clothing that people could put on.
2:5: Hannah assumes that readers will know that by the satisfied ones, she means people who formerly were satisfied in the sense that they had enough to eat. The context suggests further that they had plenty of food without having to work.
Hannah is using the term bread to represent food in general.
Hannah is speaking as if the woman she is describing has had exactly seven children.
2:6: Hannah is speaking as if people could come up from Sheol, the place of the dead. She means that the Lord can heal people who are so sick they seem almost to have died.
2:7: Hannah is speaking as if people’s social status were a physical location that they could move down from or up to.
2:8: מֵקִים מֵעָפָר דָּל מֵאַשְׁפֹּת יָרִים אֶבְיוֹן

This could mean: (1) that Hannah is using one specific circumstance of the poor and needy to represent their desperate circumstances in general; (2) that Hannah is speaking of the poor and needy as if they were mourners, to represent the way that people in this culture who were mourning would show their grief by sitting down in the dust of the ground or in a trash heap.
In this culture, offering a person a prestigious place to sit was a symbolic action that showed them honor and conferred high status on them.

Hannah is speaking as if a seat of honor were something that these people could inherit as if it were property. She means that people will consider a seat of honor to be their seat, in other words, that they have the right to sit in such seats.
לַיהוָה מְצֻקֵי אֶרֶץ וַיָּשֶׁת עֲלֵיהֶם תֵּבֵל

Hannah is speaking as if the earth were a building that had pillars supporting it. Speaking from the perspective of her culture, she is describing how the Lord structured his creation to ensure that the world would be a stable place.
2:9: Hannah is using one part of people, their feet, to mean all of them in the act of walking, which represents living.
Hannah is using the term silenced to represent that the wicked will die, since people make no further sounds after they die.
Hannah is using the term darkness to represent the abode of the dead, which her culture considered to be a very dark place.
2:10: Hannah is using the first thing that she feels the Lord would do when coming to judge and punish his enemies, make thunder in the sky, to mean all that he would do. In this culture, people regarded thunder as something that could indicate that the Lord was about to act powerfully. In 7:10, for example, the Lord thunders against the Philistines and defeats them when they attack the Israelites.
Hannah is speaking of the ends or extreme limits of the earth in order to mean them and everything in between.
Hannah is using the term earth to represent the people who live on the earth.
See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of why Hannah speaks of a king even though Israel had no king at this time.
Hannah is using the term anointed one to represent the king she has just mentioned, since in this culture men were anointed with oil when they became kings.
2:11: As the Introduction to 1 Samuel discusses, here as in many other instances throughout the book, the author is using the name of a person to represent him and other people who are associated with or accompanying him.
The author assumes that readers will know that by the boy, he means Samuel.
See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of why the author may say at here rather than the usual “to.”
2:13: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
The author assumes that readers will know that by the priests, he means specifically Eli’s sons.
The phrase translated as sacrificing a sacrifice is a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
The author assumes that readers will know that this refers to the meat from the sacrifice that the worshipers were boiling.
A fork is a utensil with prongs or tines used for picking up food.
2:14: בַכִּיּוֹר אוֹ בַדּוּד אוֹ בַקַּלַּחַת אוֹ בַפָּרוּר
These are all different kinds of cooking vessels.
The author assumes that readers will understand that the servant would bring the meat back to the priest, who would take it for himself.
2:16: The person sacrificing is using a common expression of his culture to mean that something should happen that very day, with the implication that it should happen right away.
The person sacrificing is using one part of the priest, his soul, to mean all of him in the act of wanting something.
2:17: The author assumes that readers will know that by the young men he means Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas.
See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of why the author may say at here rather than “to.”
2:18: See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of why the author may say at here rather than “to.”
Wearing an ephod was a symbolic action that showed Samuel was serving as a priest.
2:19: The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
2:20: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word say tells what Eli did in order to bless.
Eli is speaking as if children were seed that could be planted and grown.
Eli is using the term request to represent Samuel, whom Hannah requested from the Lord.
2:21: The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that the Lord helped Hannah.
The author is using the term with the Lord to represent the place where the Israelites worshiped the Lord.
2:22: The author is making an overstatement for emphasis.
The author is speaking in a polite way about a matter that is usually private.
These were women who helped with various tasks at the sanctuary.
2:23: Eli is using the question form for emphasis.
Eli assumes that his sons will know he means the Israelites who have been bringing sacrifices.
2:24: Eli is expressing a positive meaning by using a negative word together with a term that is the opposite of his intended meaning.
2:25: Eli is using the question form for emphasis.
The author is using the term voice to represent what Eli was saying.
See the discussion in the Introduction to 1 Samuel of the author’s use of the term listen to mean “obey.”
2:26: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word going tells in what way Samuel was growing.
The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that both the Lord and people approved of Samuel.
2:27: הֲנִגְלֹה נִגְלֵיתִי אֶל־בֵּית אָבִיךָ בִּהְיוֹתָם בְּמִצְרַיִם לְבֵית פַּרְעֹה
The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
The Lord is using the term father to mean “ancestor.” He is referring specifically to Eli’s ancestor Aaron.
The Lord is using the term house to represent all the household or family of Eli’s ancestor Aaron.
2:28: The Lord assumes that Eli will know what he means by the phrase to go up on my altar. This could mean: (1) that the Lord chose the family of Aaron to do specific work at his altar; (2) that the Lord chose the family of Aaron to offer sacrifices on his altar.
The Lord is using the term house to represent the household or family of Aaron, and in this context specifically his descendants.
When the Lord says all, he means “some of every,” not everything entirely.
See the discussion in the Introduction to 1 Samuel of this use of the expression the sons of a person to mean the nation or tribe that consists of his descendants.
2:29: The Lord is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Eli and his sons were treating his sacrifices with disrespect.
The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.

In other contexts, the words sacrifice and offering can refer to two different things. But here the Lord is using them synonymously in a phrase that expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word offering tells what kind of sacrifice the Lord means.
2:30: The Lord is using a common expression of this culture to express horror at the idea he has just described.
2:31: As the Introduction to 1 Samuel discusses, the Lord is using the word Behold to focus Eli’s attention on what he is about to say.
The Lord is using the term days to represent a future time.
The Lord is speaking as if Eli’s strength and his family’s strength were each an arm that could be cut off. Strength, in turn, represents in this context the vigorous young men of a family.
2:32: The Lord is using the term house to represent Eli’s family.
The Lord is using the term days to represent time in general.
2:33: The Lord is speaking as if he would cut off people from life.
The Lord is using parts of Eli and his descendants, their eyes and souls, to mean all of them in the act of weeping and grieving.
The Lord is using the term increase to represent to further members who will be born into Eli’s family.
The specific term that the Lord uses here for men indicates young men.
2:34: וְזֶה־לְּךָ הָאוֹת אֲשֶׁר יָבֹא אֶל־שְׁנֵי בָנֶיךָ אֶל־חָפְנִי וּפִינְחָס
The Lord is speaking of this sign as if it were a living thing that could come to Eli.
2:35: The Lord is speaking as if he would raise up a priest to a height or to a standing position.
The terms heart and soul mean similar things, representing in this context inward desires. The Lord is using the two terms together for emphasis.
The Lord is speaking as if he would construct a physical house for this new priest.
The Lord is using the term days to represent time in general.
2:36: The Lord is using the term house to represent Eli’s family.
Bowing down was a symbolic action that expressed submission and indicated need.
The Lord is using specific small amounts to represent money and food in general.
The Lord is using one specific thing that people need to do to live, eating bread, to mean earning a living in general.
3:1: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
וּדְבַר־יְהוָה הָיָה יָקָר בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין חָזוֹן נִפְרָץ
The author may be using two types of revelation, a word and a vision, to represent revelation in general, which would also include such things as dreams, signs, etc.
The author is using the term word to represent what the Lord said by using words.
The author is using the term days to represent a specific time, since time is made up of days.
The author is speaking as if a vision were a physical thing that could be spread.
3:2: The author is using the term day to represent a specific time.
ועינו הֵחֵלּוּ כֵהוֹת לֹא יוּכַל לִרְאוֹת
The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
ועינו הֵחֵלּוּ כֵהוֹת לֹא יוּכַל לִרְאוֹת
These two phrases mean basically the same thing.
The author is using the term eyes to represent.
3:3: By the lamp of God, the author means the lamp that the law of Moses commanded the Israelites in Exodus 27:21 to keep burning in the tent of meeting all night long.
The author is referring to the lamp still burning to represent that it was still night, since this lamp only burned at night.
3:7: וּשְׁמוּאֵל טֶרֶם יָדַע אֶת־יְהוָה וְטֶרֶם יִגָּלֶה אֵלָיו דְּבַר־יְהוָה
The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
The expression did not … know the Lord has a different meaning here than it has in 2:12.
The author is using the term word to represent what the Lord would have said by using words.
3:9: Samuel assumes that the Lord will understand that by listening, he means he will obey.
3:10: The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that the Lord spoke this time just as he had the other times.
3:11: The Lord is using a physical sensation that people will have (their ears will tingle) to represent the emotion that people will feel when they hear this news.
3:12: The author is using the term day to represent a specific time.
The Lord is speaking as if what he said he would do were something physical that he could raise up.
The Lord is using the term house to represent a family, since members of a family often live in the same house.
The Lord is speaking of two things in order to mean them and everything in between.
3:13: The Lord is providing background information to help Samuel understand why he is judging and punishing Eli’s family.

The sense of the reflexive form here is not that Eli’s sons have actually spoken curses against themselves. Rather, the Lord means that their actions have been so bad that these sons deserve to be cursed.
3:14: אִם־יִתְכַּפֵּר עֲוֺן בֵּית־עֵלִי בְּזֶבַח וּבְמִנְחָה עַד־עוֹלָם

Following the custom of this culture, the Lord is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). The implication is that if the first part of the condition were met, something very bad would happen, so it is certain that the first part of the condition will not be met.
אִם־יִתְכַּפֵּר עֲוֺן בֵּית־עֵלִי בְּזֶבַח וּבְמִנְחָה עַד־עוֹלָם
The Lord is speaking as if iniquity were a living thing that could cover itself. He is using the idea of covering to represent atonement for sin.
3:15: The author is using one specific action that Samuel performed, opening these doors, to represent all of his regular duties.
See the discussion of these doors in the Introduction to this chapter.
The author assumes that readers will understand that Samuel did not tell Eli about the vision because he was afraid to do so.

By the vision, the author seems to be implying that the Lord appeared visibly to Samuel when he came and said the things he records in 3:11–14. The author’s statement in 3:10 that the Lord “came and stationed himself” next to Samuel suggests that this was the case.
3:17: Eli is using the term word to represent what the Lord said by using words.
Eli is speaking as if information were a physical object that Samuel might hide.
Eli is swearing an oath. Following the custom of his culture, he is asking God to do to Samuel the things God said he would do to Eli and his family if Samuel does not answer him truthfully.
Eli is using a common expression of his culture to emphasize that he wants Samuel to tell him everything.

Eli is making an overstatement for emphasis. By saying that he does not want Samuel to leave out a single word of what the Lord said, he means that he wants Samuel to tell him all of the content of what the Lord said.
Eli is using the term word in the second instance in the verse to represent what the Lord said by using words.
3:18: וַיַּגֶּד־לוֹ שְׁמוּאֵל אֶת־כָּל־הַדְּבָרִים וְלֹא כִחֵד מִמֶּנּוּ
These two phrases mean basically the same thing.
3:19: The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that the Lord helped Samuel.

The author is speaking as if words were physical objects that could fall to the ground. The suggestion is that Samuel’s words were never lost or ruined as things do that people drop or let fall, in other words, what he said always came true.
The author is using the term words to represent what Samuel said by using words.
3:20: The author is speaking of two cities at the opposite ends of Israel’s territory in order to mean them and all the territory in between them.
That term could have the same meaning here.
3:21: The author is using the term word to represent what the Lord said by using words.
4:1: The author is using the term word to represent what Samuel said by using words.
4:2: The word translated was struck here, meaning “was defeated,” is different from the one in the next sentence translated they struck, meaning “they killed.”
See the discussion of the term struck in the Introduction to 1 Samuel.
4:3: לָמָּה נְגָפָנוּ יְהוָה הַיּוֹם לִפְנֵי פְלִשְׁתִּים

There is an implicit answer to this question in what the elders decide to do the rest of this verse. They feel as if the Lord himself has defeated them, and they believe the reason is that they did not bring the Box of the Covenant with them into battle. See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of why they believed this.
See the discussion in the Introduction to 1 Samuel of the use of the word “hand” to represent power. The elders are using the word palm here to mean the same thing.
4:4: וְשָׁם שְׁנֵי בְנֵי־עֵלִי עִם … חָפְנִי וּפִינְחָס
The word there does not refer to Shiloh but to the place to which the Israelites brought the Box of the Covenant.
4:5: For emphasis, the author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
4:6: The author is speaking of the Box of the Lord as if it were a living thing that could have come into the camp on its own.
4:7: In this culture, the current day was considered the first day, the previous day was considered the second day, and the day before that was considered the third day.
4:8: מִי יַצִּילֵנוּ מִיַּד הָאֱלֹהִים הָאַדִּירִים הָאֵלֶּה
The Philistines are using the question form for emphasis.
The Philistine soldiers are speaking as if the Lord had actually struck or hit the Egyptians with these plagues.
The Philistines are making an overstatement for emphasis.
See the discussion of this phrase in the Introduction to this chapter.
4:9: The Philistines are using the term men to represent people who are courageous. The implication is that strong, experienced, full-grown men would be courageous in situations where weaker, inexperienced boys and youths would not.
These two phrases mean similar things. The Philistines are using the two terms together for emphasis.
The phrase be men and fight expresses a single idea. The word fight tells more about what men would or should do in this situation.
4:10: The author assumes that readers will know that by fought, he means that the Philistines fought courageously, as they told themselves they had to do.
The author is using a man to his tent as a common expression of his culture to mean that the soldiers stopped their military campaign altogether and each of them went back to his home and family.
The author is using the term fell to mean that these soldiers were killed in the battle, to represent the way they fell to the ground when they died.
4:12: Tearing his clothes and putting earth on his head were symbolic actions by which this man demonstrated his great distress over the news he was bringing.
4:13: The author is using the term behold to call attention to what he is about to say.

Since the author explains in 4:15 that Eli was blind, he does not mean that Eli was literally watching the road to see whether any messengers were coming. He means that Eli was waiting for news and hoping to recognize a messenger from the sound of his arrival.
The author is using one part of Eli, his heart, to mean all of him in the act of feeling strongly.
The author is using the term city to represent the people of the city.
The author is making an overstatement for emphasis.
4:14: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word hurried tells in what way the messenger came.
4:15: The author is using a common expression of his culture to state someone’s age.

The author is using the phrase his eyes had set to describe an eye condition that was most likely cataracts. He said of Eli in 3:2 that “his eyes had begun to be dim,” that is, he could see objects only faintly. Now the cataracts had advanced to the point where his eyes no longer moved.

31:10: By this phrase, the author means that they put both Saul’s equipment and his head in their temple. The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 10:10 states that explicitly.

Putting the armor (and, apparently in this case, the head) of a defeated enemy leader in a temple or sanctuary was a symbolic action that attributed the victory over this enemy to the help of the deity whom people worshiped in that temple or sanctuary. This is what David did with Goliath’s sword and head, as the author describes in 17:54.

The city of Beth Shan was a few miles west of the Jordan River. The narrative suggests in 31:7 that the Philistines had occupied this city. By hanging on the city wall the body of the Israelite king they had killed, they were asserting that they had conquered Israelite territory extending this far.

The author is using the body of one person that the Philistines fastened to the wall, Saul’s corpse, to represent the bodies of Saul and his sons. The author indicates in 31:12 that the Philistines also fastened his sons’ bodies to the wall.
31:12: By this phrase, the author means that these men took action.
The Israelites probably burned the bodies in this instance, even though that was not their usual practice, in order to prevent any further desecration of them by the Philistines.
31:13: Sitting under a tamarisk tree was symbolic of royal status, as the story indicates in 22:6. By burying Saul under that kind of tree, the people of Jabesh Gilead were giving him royal honors in his death.
The people of Jabesh Gilead fasted seven days to show respect to Saul and to express their grief over his death.
